baskerville.A1:
Officer Is Licked By a Negro Porter
Patrolman "Nick" Flannigan was pounded until he was unconscious by Joe Baskerville, a negro porter at the Congress saloon, Fifth and Pike, at 6 o'clock. Friday morning after he had threatened to shoot the colored man. Both were taken to the police station in the patrol wagon. Chief Delaney will make an investigation of the case.

Flannigan has a night shift, and was in an intoxicated condition, it is alleged by witnesses of the fight, when he walked into the saloon and began to make trouble.

He first paid for two drinks, and then demanded a pint of whisky as a present, stating that he was a friend of Jack Condon, the owner of the place. Bartender Patrick Jennings refused to make the donation, averring that he did not have the authority.

Then it is claimed Flannigan began to abuse and curse the bartender, finally offering to thrash both him and the porter. The latter stepped out from behind the bar and said he would not stand for the abuse, and, taking off his hat, offered to fight him alone.

Flannigan crawfished and pulled a gun. Baskerville did not attack
baskerville.A2: him until he had again pocketed the weapon. Then Baskerville knocked the policeman down. There was a fight. Baskerville finally took the officer's gun from him, and when Flannigan struck him with a brass knuckle he also took that away. Flannigan was game, however, and was knocked down 20 times and driven clear to the sidewalk before he rurrendered. By this time the police had been notified and Officers Kent and Day took both men into custody. Both were bleeding profusely, and Flannigan was badly bruised.

A BAD NEGRO. Murdered a Man and Shot One of The Pursuing Party. Stamps, Ark., Aug. 2.—E. R. Ferguson, claim agent of the Louisiana & Arkansas railroad, was killed near Stamps today by a negro named Ike Kinney. Kinney killed a negro this morning at Stamps and escaped, and Ferguson was a member of a posse which went in search of him. The negro was encountered about three miles from Stamps, and opened fire, killing Ferguson. A reward of $500 has been offered for Kinney, and special trains have been sent to Pine Bluff, Ark., to take bloodhounds to Stamps. SECY. WILSON EXPLAINS. Tells Why He Sent His Son to Alaska on Government Business.
Washington, Aug. 2.—Secy. Wilson today issued a statement relating to a charge that his son and private secretary, Jasper Wilson, made a trip to Alaska about a year ago at the expense of the department. Secy. Wilson says the trip was made at his instance and was for the purpose of ascertaining the condition of the game there, delegates from Alaska having protested against sending anybody in there with permission to shoot and bring out trophies. The miners claimed that they lived there in the winter; that the game was a resource which often stood between them and starvation.

"I wanted to know the real facts," said the secretary, "and sent my private secretary up there. He was a salaried officer here. The department paid his actual traveling expenses, of course. I send men all over the world for information.

"Upon receipt of my private secretary's report I shut down on the granting of permits to everybody excepting persons representing the museums and other educational institutions."

JEWS ABROAD.

Dr. Danziger Arrives to Give Dept. of Labor Information.

Washington, Aug. 2.—Dr. Adolphe Danziger, formerly United States consul at Madrid, arrived here today to lay before the department of commerce and labor memoranda concerning the condition of the Jews abroad, the information being gathered at the request of the department for use in the bureau of immigration in dealing with that class of immigrants. "In England, Germany and Russia," said Dr. Danziger, in reviewing his observations today, "what struck me most notably was the hopeful views the Jews take of America. "The people I met were hoping that the president would take the opportunity that presented itself to induce the Russian government to grant them freedom or at least to give them equal rights in Russia. BLOODY Record Made By a Bad Negro In Arkansas. HE HAD KILLED TWO PEOPLE AND WOUNDED FOUR OTHERS WHEN SHOT BY POSSE. PURSUED BY SPECIAL TRAIN.
Little Rock, Ark., Aug. 3.—A special from Lewisville, Ark., says:

After killing two persons, seriously and probably fatally shooting two others, one a woman, and less seriously shooting two more, Ike Kinney, a desperate negro, was killed in a river bottom at Doella, six miles south of Lewisville, at noon to-day, after a hot fight with a posse of citizens that had surrounded him. His bloody record for twenty-four hours is:

August 2 (morning), killed a negro at Stamps.

August 2 (afternoon), killed E. R. Ferguson, claim agent of the Louisiana and Arkansas railroad, member of a posse three miles from Stamps.

August 3 (3 a. m.), seriously shot Mrs. Stewart, of Greensburg, and Mr. Stewart, her husband.

August 3 (noon), shot Alvil Barham through the neck and shot a finger off one of C. F. Nash's hands.

**Left Trail of Gore.**

Kinney, who had killed a negro at Stamps on Wednesday, fled, and while being pursued by a posse shot and killed E. R. Ferguson. This augmented the feeling against the negro, but to cap the bloody climax, it was learned that a man named Stewart and his wife from Greensburg had been shot by Kinney at 3 o'clock this morning, three miles from Lewisville. Without a word of warning, the negro opened with his Winchester, firing four shots and shooting Mrs. Stewart through the breast and her husband through the side. Mrs. Stewart, who is now at Stamps, was seriously wounded. After shooting Mr. and Mrs. Stewart, the negro told them that he thought they were members of a posse, and assured them he was very sorry that he had fired on them.

Early this morning about twenty-five men with dogs started out on Kinney's trail. They got the first clew from a man on a river farm south of this city, who told them that a negro had come to his house that morning and asked for a drink of water and to be taken across Red river.

Killed By a Posse.

A few members of the searching party finally located Kinney in a bottom near Doella, which is a plantation post-office. Word was at once sent to Lewisville and a posse started shortly before noon on a special train for the scene of the expected battle.

As soon as the posse had arrived and begun to close in on the negro, he opened fire. C. F. Nash lost a finger. Alvin Barham was shot through the neck and seriously wounded. Then W. C. Nash shot a bullet in the negro and tumbled him over dead. The posse and the body of the negro were brought back to Stamps on a special train.

Fifteen hundred dollars had been offered for the capture of Kinney, dead or alive.

NEVER MISSED TEAM

LIVERYMAN RENTED RIG TO SALESMAN.

KEPT IT SIXTEEN MONTHS.

Bill Footed Up $485—Charged With Using Loaded Cane On His Brother.

Lexington, Ky., Aug. 3.—[Special.]—After keeping a horse and buggy which he had rented from G. H. Goodrich for sixteen months N. B. Duncan, a traveling salesman for the Magic Food Company, of Chattanooga, Tenn., drove up in front of the stable last night. Mr. Goodrich was unable to recognize the horse and vehicle as his and even declared that he had not missed either the animal or the rig. He said Duncan had been in the habit of renting rigs almost weekly from him, and just supposed that the last one rented had not been returned. Duncan explained that he had been all through the South with the horse and buggy, and both the animal and buggy bore proof to the statement. While Mr. Goodrich was surprised at the return of the rig. Duncan was equally surprised over the amount of the livery bill which Goodrich made out to him and which amounted to $485, or about three times the value of the horse and vehicle.

Funeral of Mrs. Gormley.

The body of Mrs. Margaret Gormley, of this city, who died suddenly in Cincinnati Wednesday morning, was brought here to-day and the funeral services will be held Friday morning at St. Paul's Catholic church. Mrs. Gormley was the mother of Miss Mamye Gormley, who returned yesterday from a trip to Europe, where she had been as the guest of a Cincinnati paper, having received the most votes in the contest for the most popular clerk of this city.

**Thrown From Her Buggy.**

Mrs. Stella Wood, living on the Mt. Liberty pike, was run into while driving on the road last night, her vehicle being upset, throwing her to the ground and dragging her some distance before the horse could be stopped. Mrs. Wood stated that she was run into by three drunken men who were driving along at a rapid gait and who never stopped to see if she was injured.

**Brother Swore Out Warrant.**

John H. Stamper, proprietor of a grocery on Georgetown street, was arrested this morning on a warrant sworn out by his brother, Asa Stamper, charging him with assault. The younger Stamper alleges that his brother struck him over the head with a loaded cane while they were trying to have a settlement. When Stamper appeared before Magistrate Oldham last night and asked for the warrant he was very weak from the blow and had to be taken home in a carriage.

IN DELIRIUM SAW AIRSHIP THEN SEVERED AN ARTERY.

Petersburg, Ind., Aug. 3.—[Special.]—While in a delirium to-day Alex. Amos imagined he saw an airship from which people were firing at him. He grabbed a butcher knife and severed an artery in his arm. He will die.

Richmond, Ky., Aug. 3.—[Special.]—John Ballard, assistant postmaster of the local post-office, was arrested last night by Secret Service men while in the act of rifling the United States mail. For about two months past small amounts have been missing from registered letters and in consequence of which Government detectives were detailed to investigate this shortage.

Last night young Ballard was seen to open several packages and secrete the contents on his person. He was promptly apprehended and brought before United States Commissioner W. C. Bennett, of this city, by whom he was released on $300 bond to await the action of the Federal grand jury in October.

The incident has created a sensation, as Mr. Ballard is a popular and prominent young man. He is a nephew of both Postmaster C. C. Wallace, of this city, and Bland Ballard, Chief Deputy in the Collector's office at Danville. The amount of his alleged pilferings total about $52.

BIGAMY IS CHARGED.

Jas. F. Hayden, Who Deserted Wife and Children In Louisville, Under Arrest.

Elizabethtown, Aug. 3.—[Special.]—Capt. W. C. Elliott, a well-known detective of this place, has just worked out a sensational case against James F. Hayden, formerly of Elizabethtown, and as a result Hayden is in jail at Selmer, Tenn., charged with bigamy. The preliminary trial is set for next Tuesday. Several years ago Hayden married a Miss Wiseman, of Hardin. It is now alleged that he deserted his wife and eight children in Louisville last October, going to Tennessee, where he was known as Frank Hayden. On March 16 of the current year he married Miss Kittie Perkins, of Stantonville, a graduate of Hamilton College, Lexington, Ky., and worth about $15,000. It is charged that Hayden, after trying vainly to get her fortune into his own hands, so conducted himself as to arouse suspicion, with the result that Detective Elliott was called in to investigate the case. While in Kentucky Hayden was a stock dealer and is well known in this and adjoining counties. Capt. Elliott and Mrs. Hayden, of Louisville, the prisoner's first wife, and from whom he has never been divorced, will attend the examining trial Tuesday as witnesses.

NEGRO MAN IS SHOT BY POLICEMAN RAY
DAN HOWARD ATTEMPTED TO ES-
CAPE AND RECEIVED WOUND IN
THE ABDOMEN—HE MAY DIE.
Dan Howard, a negro, was shot and probably fatally wounded last night about 11:30 o'clock by Policeman Ray while attempting to escape.

Policemen Ray and Elledge, while patrolling their beat last night about 11 o'clock, were told by a little negro boy that Howard had shot at his sister, Rana Stovall. The two officers immediately went to the house of the negro at Eleventh street and Fourth avenue, but before they could get the handcuffs on him he broke loose and started running up the street.

Both policemen ordered him to stop, but he did not heed their demands. Officer Ray then drew his pistol and fired three shots, one of them taking effect in the negro's abdomen. The negro was brought to the police station, but was later sent to St. Vincent's hospital. At an early hour this morning he was still living, but his chances for recovery are meagre.

A charge of assault with intent to murder was docketed against Howard.
dan-howard-1905-08-16.A2:
NEGRO MAY RECOVER.
Many Shot By Policeman Ray Has a Chance for His Life.
Dan Howard, the negro who was shot by Policeman Ray late Wednesday night, has a chance to recover from his wound, according to the physicians at the Hillman hospital.

The negro rested well yesterday and had little fever. Howard has a strong constitution and may pull through, it is said.

A charge with assault with a pistol with intent to commit murder is docketed against Howard, who, it is said, shot at his sister on Eleventh street and Fourth avenue just before he was arrested. He was trying to escape from Policemen Ray and Elledge when he was shot.

The ball with which the negro was wounded was of .38 calbre and passed entirely through the negro's body, entering the right side of the lower abdomen and coming out several inches lower in the back part of the hip.

Negro Doctor Ordered to Leave.
We learned a few days ago that Dr. Howard has been notified to leave Hattiesburg, not to attend law school, nor to be faithful and lawmaking citizen. He has not offended any one and the one who offended him has his color and success in his profession. The good white people who make the peaceful and law-abiding citizens be they black or white — The Barbie

The legislature should take steps on this practice in Mississippi and enact laws to prevent a set of men from perpetrating such outrages upon any other set of men be they white or black. The time has come in the South that should a Negro be doing well in any calling or profession of life and his success is antagonistic to his white brother who is engaged in the same trade or profession, they simply order him away. They give the Negro the "move-on" orders. When these orders are given you, you will have to move or die; or your business is destroyed and nobody is held responsible for your life or property. This is a shame. It is an outrage. How can this Government protect Cuba from the Spanish oppression, and cannot protect the humblest of its own citizens? We should begin protection at home and then when all of our people are safely protected look around for other worlds to conquer.

Henry C. S. Hastings and William B. Costes and about 20 others
fantry, volunteers, have sued the United States government for two months' pay for services in the Hawaiian islands during the Spanish-American war.

Warrants were sworn out against four officials and one clerk of the Western bank, Denver, which closed its doors. The men are charged with receiving deposits when they knew the Western bank was insolvent.

At Helena, Mont., Volvo, the bicycle rider with the Barnum & Bailey circus, who jumps the gap during the performance, failed to do the trick there and fell to the ground. Physicians fear he is fatally injured.

The 37 members of the Fiala-Ziegler polar expedition which have returned to safety at Honningsvaag, Norway, are all in good health, despite their privations, trying experiences and their prolonged imprisonment in the arctic, the expedition having been severed from all communication with the outside world since July, 1903.

Bishop Fitzgerald, of the Catholic diocese of Little Rock, Ark., senior bishop of the province of New Orleans, has appointed Bishop Rouxel, of New Orleans, as the temporary successor of Archbishop Chappelle.

The Kansas City inspector of weights and measures tested a number of gallon measures used by the drivers of the Standard Oil Co. in delivering oil and declared after the examination that each 15 out of 21 measures tested lacked one-half pint of holding five gallons.

Prof. Willis L. Moore, of the United States weather bureau, issued a signed statement denying all allegations of graft in the management of the weather station in the Blue Ridge mountains, near Bluemont, Va.

The Glass Bottle Blowers' association and the machine branch of the Glass Manufacturers' association came to an agreement and ended the long conference. Wages and hours same as last year.

The cruiser Galveston which arrived in Hampton Roads, Va., has been assigned by the navy department, at the instance of the state department, to transport Prof. John H. Hollander and his secretary to San Domingo.

Chief of Police Pinkham, of Passadena, Cal., arrested Mace Hitchcock, alias McHenry, and John Caster, alias John W. Roth, at Los Angeles, Cal. They are said to be wanted at Bedford, Ind., the former on the charge of attempted murder and the latter on a minor charge. The men admit their identity.

E. H. Butler, editor and proprietor of the Buffalo Evening News, was robbed of $1,400 in cash and signed checks for $400 as he alighted from a train in the Erie railroad station.

After eight hours of argument the executive heads of the Illinois coal mine operators and of the Illinois branch of the United Coal Workers gave up in despair all attempts to adjust their differences and separated.

The steamer Kanagawa, from Hong-Kong, brings news of a plot there to ship 10,000 rifles and 1,000,000 rounds of ammunition to Samar, and other unpacified districts in the Philippines.

lemuel-cannon-minneapolis-1905-08-08.A1:
CROWD D GATHERED
TO LYNCH NEGRO
ESCAPED VIOLENCE BECAUSE HE COULDN'T GET BAIL.
Man Accused of Brutal Assault on Young Girl in North Minneapolis Is Identified by His Victim—Self-Appointed Avengers Surrounded His House and Waited in Vain.
Angered at the brutality of a colored man who assaulted a young girl near Farview park last Sunday night, a crowd of more than a hundred men and boys last evening surrounded the home of Lemuel Cannon, the negro charged with the crime and organized a lynching party.

Cannon was arrested last night after being identified by the victim of the assault, and word soon spread about North and Northeast Minneapolis of the crime. A party of young men gathered near Twentieth avenue N and, after a hurried consultation, started for the negro's home at 338 Quincy street NE, thinking that he would be released on bail and would return.

While on the way across the river the lynching party gradually increased, and all along the line the bystanders were told the object of the organization.

They went quietly but determinedly to avenge the wrong done the little girl, whom many of them knew. Police officers who saw the crowd thought nothing of it because of the quiet and order, but two men in the center carried two strong ropes which they had obtained at a livery stable.

For some time the mob waited in the vicinity of the house for the return of the man. Finally one of the men telephoned to Central station and learned that Cannon could not get bail.

Then most of the men went home, but a few remained in case they had been misinformed.

When Cannon was arraigned in court today several men who were in the crowd last night were on hand to hear the proceedings. He was held for examination in $1,000 bail.

"We will certainly get him if he is released on bail," said one man as he passed down the elevator this morning. "The best thing for him to do is to stay in jail."
Cannon's Heinous Crime.

Cannon, the accused man, who is an ex-convict, was locked up at the North Side station yesterday charged with the assault.

It is alleged that while the girl was sitting on a bench in Farview park with a boy friend, Cannon accosted them and, claiming to be an officer, drove the boy from the park and detained the girl. With the boy out of sight, he threatened the girl with arrest and imprisonment unless she submitted to him. Frightened almost to insensibility, the girl yielded and later in the evening she went home and there told her story to her parents.

The matter was at once laid before the police, and yesterday Detective Tom Gallagher, Sergeant Ginsberg and Patrolman Hall arrested Cannon on the charge. The girl identified the prisoner as her assailant and the police say they have other incriminating evidence.

Cannon has already served two terms in the penitentiary, one for burglary and one for criminal assault.

DEVINE UNMOVED
BY ARRAIGNMENT
SLAYER OF WILLIAM WALLACE ENTERS PLEA OF NOT GUILTY.
Makes Oath That He Is Without Funds and Court Will Appoint an Attorney to Defeend Him—Grand Jury's Grist of Indictments Calls Forth Many Pleas of "Not Guilty."
John Devine slouched up to the bar of justice in Judge F. C. Brooks' courtroom today, and without the slightest show of feeling listened to the reading of an indictment charging him with the murder of William Wallace, at Greenwood, Aug. 25. He pleaded not guilty and his trial was set for Sept. 26. He swore that he had no money and Judge Brooks will appoint a lawyer to advise him. Devine was roughly clad and is to all appearances a day laborer.

Devine has confessed to the killing of Wallace. He says he was drunk when he stabbed Wallace and did not know what he had done until long after his victim's death. It is probable that Devine will plead guilty to manslaughter and County Attorney Al J. Smith has intimated that the state will be satisfied with such a plea.

Frank Kalmer and William Doole, two of the burglars whose kit of tools and dynamite struck fear into the hearts of the local detective at the time of the arrest, were arraigned on three indictments charging grand larceny in the first and burglary in the third degree. Clarence Warmelin, the third member of the gang, was indicted, but was not arraigned today. He has turned state's evidence and will probably get off easier than his pals. policeman-john-elliott-new-york-1905-08-.A1:
NEGRO ASKS SQUARE DEAL.
Says Low Whites Are Equally to Blame for Race Riots—Would Carry Arms.
To the Editor of The Tribune.

Sir: I have read with interest your recent editorial on the race riots in New-York, and would like to say a few words on the same subject.

Three of our ministers, the Rev. Messrs. Simms, E. M. McDaniell and N. S. Epps, recently consulted with Police Commissioner McAdoo, and presented facts concerning the riots between whites and blacks in the Sixties. Mr. McAdoo, among other things, told the ministers that he would do everything in his power to protect the law-abiding orderly and honest people of both races.

That part of the statement is both commendable and appreciated, but what chance has a colored man who is not looking for trouble when attacked by a crowd of white ruffians, if he hasn't a pistol to stand them off until assistance comes? Now, the respectable element of our race does not wish to carry firearms or weapons, but in times like these it seems as if it ought to be permissible for respectable colored men to carry some weapon for self-protection, especially those that live in the districts where the riots have occurred.

Mrs. Christopher, the colored woman whose husband was shot, said that her husband was innocent of any connection with the riots, and that she believes the policemen are in league with the whites and beat the colored men on the least provocation.

The writer believes the statement of Mrs. Christopher. The police do seem to be in league with the whites, as alleged. When a policeman arrives at a fight the first person pounced upon is a negro.

Commissioner McAdoo issued a statement, wherein he appointed a committee to investigate the causes of these riots, and also to suggest remedies to prevent them in the future. Now, I think the initial step should be to have a sufficient number of policemen on patrol in all these districts and streets where riots are likely to occur, especially in the Sixties, so as to put a stop immediately to any disturbance that may arise and culminate in a riot; also to keep the corners clear of the loafers of each race.

Prejudice and a deep hatred for the negroes are the sole cause of all these riots and disturbances. Why, I am unable to explain. Take the riot of last Friday night; its cause was just a simple matter. A negro volunteered to assist an old white pedler whom some white boys were molesting; the boys turned on the negro, who fought back, causing the riot. Now, you don't blame the negroes for this riot, do you?

The remedy for all these racial frictions rests solely with the police and real estate owners of this city. There are hundreds of houses being erected to-day, and there are hardly five built es-
The remedy for all these racial frictions rests solely with the police and real estate owners of this city. There are hundreds of houses being erected to-day, and there are hardly five built especially for colored people. Why is it? The colored tenant pays his rent just as regularly as any other.

At present the respectable class of colored people are compelled to live in localities where the bad element predominates, and when riots and disturbances break out the public judges the good negro as it does those of the vilest character and type.

Commissioner McAdoo and Mayor McClellan ought to see that these race riots should cease.

Extra policemen should be assigned to these blocks wherein whites and blacks reside, and they should keep a close watch to prevent clashes between the two races.

The sentiment of the colored people is partly voiced in an editorial in The New-York Tribune of July 16, which says in part:

. . . The negro is here as a weak and, to some extent, an ostracized element in our population. He is the "under dog" in our industrial as well as in our social system. It is, therefore, all the more important that we should give him a "square deal." We should not put respectable blacks and criminal blacks on the same level. We should set the example which we urge on the South, of encouraging the good negro while discouraging the bad one. Least of all should we put in practice the theory—involved in every race war—that a man is to be judged not by his individual conduct, but by the color of his skin, be it white or black or yellow.

That's all we want—a "square deal;" no more, no less.

If there be any doubt about this question let the Editor of The Tribune, or one of his reporters, disguise himself as a negro and pass by some of these corners or through some of these streets wherein the whites that are always looking for trouble predominate, and see for himself.

BENJAMIN PALMER LADSON.
No. 222 West 64th-st., New-York City.
policeman-john-elliott-new-york-1905-08-.A2:
EVEN DEVERY WHACKS POLICE
And Arenes Favorable Sentiment in
Industrial Quarters.

The discrimination which the police enforced against Afro-Americans in the recent "race riots" in New York city was no fragrant as to stir up the indignation of even ex-Chief of Police William S. Devery. In an interview with the New York Times of July 20 he said, when charged with being a friend of Captain Cooney, for whose incompetence or worse during the riots," Commissioner McAdoo has transferred him to another district:

"Captain Cooney would not turn a hand for me. He is Tom Smith and Tammany Hall body and soul. While there is all this talk going on about Negro riots on the West Side, let me tell you that there has been no such thing as a Negro riot in many years. Plain-giving, biggest Negro 'longshoremen,' however, on their way home from work have been beaten for a month past by bhoods along 10th avenue, and have been left in the gutters for dead, and no police to help them. It's time that the police stopped clubbing Negroes, who are human beings like ourselves, and if we believe our early teachings there would be no Negroes were it not for Cain and Abel.

"Treat Negroes, Japanese, and Chinamen all alike when it comes to police protection, for they are all human, and a strict investigation should be made as to the recent clubbing of Negroes."
policeman-john-elliott-new-york-1905-08-.A3:
"Meanwhile it is in order to point out that Captain Cooney's case is the latest instance of the relative futility of the practice of, transferring officers because of neglect or incompetence. In the bill of the Committee of Nine prepared last year was provided that remorsals or reduction in commission to perform duty, through neglect or incompetence. Such a provision would give the commissioner a certain degree of

definite power, which would carry with it a corresponding degree of definite responsibility, and it should be put in the law. At the same time we are convinced that the commissioner already has enough power to secure much better discipline than prevails. A mere change in the field of action is not an adequate way of making a man do better." The New York Evening Post, which had the same objective detention of the behavior of the police in the "reits," endorses the position of Mr. Dewey and reiterates its demand for a searching investigation of the whole situation:

"Whatever else may be said of Devery, his knowledge of police conditions is beyond challenge. Hence his views on the so-called Negro riots in this city are of value. He is reported to-day as saying precisely what the observers beat acquainted with conditions on the West Side have been declaring to be the truth: "We have been beaten up, such thing as a Negro-riot in many years. Plain-going, honest Negro 'longshoremen, however on their way home from work have been beaten for a month past by floodlums along 10th avenue, and have been left in the gutters for dead, and no police to help them. It's time that the police stopped clubbing Negroes, who are human beings, we ourselves," he said, in a strict investigation of the actions of the police, and when he says that police clubbing is almost never necessary, it is worth while putting his opinion by for future reference. Mr. McAdoo has taken one step of importance—the transferring of Captain Gooney from this precinct to another. This captain was known to be unfriendly to the Negroes. Police violence in the city should not stop there. The public is entitled not only to a searching investigation into recent outbreaks, but also to a careful, unbiased study of the whole situation, so that such occurrences as riots may not again disguce the city."

CALL TO MEET AT DETROIT.
EIGHTH ANNUAL SESSION OF AFRO-AMERICAN COUNCIL.

Necessity for the Coming Meeting Strongly Set Forth - Diffranchise the Chief Issue - Runs of Membership - Three Days' Session Beginning August 28 - First Bonus of the Council Recited - Special Mates to Detroit - Preparing to Entertain Delegates.

The following call, signed by officers of the Afro-American Council, has been received by THE AGE with the request that it be given publication:

"To the members of the National Afro-American Council, delegates from local Councils and affiliated organizations, such as colleges, benevolent societies, newspapers and other race organizations, Greeting:

"The eighth annual session of the National and Afro-American Council will be held at Detroit, Mich., on August 30 and 31, and September 1. 1905. The recent dangerous, and, on the part of the police officers, scandalous, race riots in New York city, the lynching of seven Negroes at Watkinsville, Georgia, the demoniac ravings of Governor Vardaman of Mississippi and the "Jim Crowing" of the street cars of the leading cities of the South, call loudly to the derelict members of the Afro-American Council and the friends of fair play to arouse themselves and to do something to check this onslaught upon their civil and political rights.

"The hostility upon the part of the enemies of the race has been so persistent that many of our friends have become timid and indifferent in our defence. It is with the view of combating this opposition of our enemies, strengthening the hands of our friends and working for the absolute undoing of all discriminations against the race, that this meeting is to be held, and we ask the hearty co-operation of every Afro-American who is interested in the welfare of the race.

HANDSOME APARTMENTS. 4 and 5 Rooms and Bath. Steam Heat and Hot Water Supply. Open Plumbing. Rents Moderate. Janitor on Premises. SAMUEL A. KELSEY, Agent 363 Lennox Avenue

Local Branch of National News League Taking Up Police Battles in "Race Riot" - Personnel League to safeguard Civil Rights Projected by Leading New Yorkers.

The brutality of the metropolitan police in the all-called "race riot" has stirred up the indignation of Afro-American New Yorkers to the sticking point, that is, they are making practical preparations not only to punish this offense against the race, but to discourage and, if possible, prevent such offenses in the future. The initiative in this matter was taken by Her. Dr. Rypks and Mr. Gilchrist Stewart, and the local branch of the National Negro Business League, together with committees from the Colored Republican club and the Colored Democratic club, and the various pastors, instigated by these gentlemen, is taking practical steps to organize a permanent Afro-American defense league. Two meetings for this purpose have already been held, with the result that a committee has been appointed to nominate officers and plan the details of a permanent organization. This committee will report tonight to a called meeting of the various bodies at 138 West 53d street, the meeting place of the local Business League.
policeman-john-elliott-new-york-1905-08-.A6:
RACE RIOTS.
We have refrained from commenting on the New York race riot for the reason that we have long since learned that there are two sides to every case, and we did not care to run the risk of blaming one side for what might have been the fault of the other. But it seems that the returns are all in, and this riot, like many others, was prompted alone by the cussedness of white toughs. But this fact was not sufficient to keep the chief of police from distorting all the facts in the case. This is nothing new, nor is such civic mendacity confined to New York. It is just this thing that furnishes whatever there is of a discouraging feature of these race troubles. It seems to indicate that there are those who do not care to know the truth about these troubles, or that if they did know, it would make little or no difference in the position assumed. And the other side of this means that, whatever the cause, or wherever the blame, the Negro must stand as the guilty man in any of these race conflicts. This means, in turn, that the tough, rowdy Negro's sure to get into trouble, and that the well behaved and gentlemanly Negro need not expect on this account to keep out of trouble. And when it gets to this point, it means that, if the known offenders are white row-dies, they need not fear punishment for the reason that none is at all likely to be inflicted. Where the case is reversed the Negro gets off easy if he lands in the workhouse or the penetentiary. So there you are at Devil's Gap. Is this the way things are to terminate? This depends on how long it takes to get the gang together. It describes how these youngsters begin with gravel, and, if necessary, end by using stones in driving away any straggling son of Ham who may have shown such poor
few hours, and sometimes for only a few minutes. This depends on how long it takes to get the gang together. It describes how these youngsters begin with gravel, and, if necessary, end by using stones in driving away any straggling son of Ham who may have shown such poor taste as to have entered this measely little village. It is related as though this was but a bit of youthful firmness used in carrying out the customs of their fathers. Since looking this village up we have about reached the conclusion that a black man who had no more sense than to want to stop in that place ought to be run out of it. policeman-john-elliott-new-york-1905-08-.A7:
RACE RIOTS IN NEW
YORK NOT INFREQUENT
SOUTHLAND NOT ONLY PLACE OF INTERNECINE WARFARE
Three in as Many Weeks, When Whites Nearly Murder Blacks—Consump- tive Colony Near the City—Im- mense Contract for Steel Bridge
Special Correspondence of The Herald.
NEW YORK, Aug. 1.—Three times in as many weeks and in as many different sections of the city there have been serious race riots with results which showed clearly there is no essential difference in the feeling between the white and the negro races in New York and that which exists in any other part of the country.
Rioting between whites and blacks is no new thing here, although it was a novelty five years ago this summer, when New Yorkers witnessed one of the most serious race riots which ever was seen in the country.
Then, in a ten-hour running fight, which started in Hell's Kitchen and extended over the entire West Side, from Fourteenth to Fifty-ninth street, negroes were dragged from their homes and from street cars to have their heads beaten in or to be strung from lampposts. The net result was nearly a dozen dead and fully 500 injured.

With all the talk against race prejudice, which is indulged in by so many white men, the feeling between the races is intense, as the police records so clearly show. For the last four or five years the police have been kept busy looking after the regions where the tenements of whites and negroes are close by. The slightest pretext serves to start a fight, and once started, whites and blacks swarm from their respective quarters, while stones, clubs and razors, to say nothing of more than a few revolvers, all add to the gaiety of nations.

Five years ago the big race riot started through the stabbing of a white policeman by a negro desperado, whose paramour was arrested by the policeman.

The latter died and the negro fled the city, but on the day of the policeman's funeral some of his neighbors threw things from their windows at a couple of negroes who were watching the funeral procession start. The negroes resented this, and in an instant the general fight was on so fiercely it took over 1000 policemen ten hours to quell it. Even then the real scattering of the mob was accomplished only by a hard rainstorm during the early hours of the following morning.

One of the latest riots started with an insulting remark of a negro at a passing white man; another started because a negro resented the gibes of some white boys playing ball, while the third was caused by a negro refusing to make way on the street to allow a white woman to pass.

All of the riots were in tenement districts where negro tenements had crept in among the white tenements. But in the light of these events no New Yorker can afford to slur an other region for the lynching of negroes or for riots which mean the terrorization of the blacks.

By fall this city will have in operation one of the finest tracts in the country for the care and treatment of consumptives. It is located in Oranges county, and the land, which consists of 1200 acres, is to cost the city $250,000. Already the appropriation has been made, and the city is now proceeding with the necessary steps to take title.

The land is located well up in the Catskill mountains. At present there are forty farm houses on it, and all are to be fitted up as the homes of patients which the city will admit to the big consumptive camp. Fully 400 patients can be accommodated within a month after the city gets its title to the property. The land is 1200 feet above sea level, and is pronounced by physicians who have been over the ground as the finest possible site for the establishment of an institution to fight the ravages of tuberculosis.

In spite of New York's complacency it has difficulties of this sort, and very real they are. The "bad niggers" element in the metropolis is larger than in any but very thickly settled negro sections, with the difference that New York's "bad niggers" often have a lot of money and assume to be people of "pull" and power. Any difference with a white man solidifies the negro group and on the other hand, white reprobates take every occasion to rebuke the clannishness of the colored men. The ordinance against firearms is everywhere ignored in New York, as each batch of arrests, with the resulting search, abundantly proves. It is a curious fact that guns are thickest in the "quarters," in those sections of the city where races are distinctively emphasized—in the negro, Italian and French districts, for example, the knife playing an important part among the Italians. Razors are no longer a civilized weapon among the negroes. The revolver is the accepted instrument of rebuke, and, in view of this fact, the police know what to expect at a race row. They know also that such a row will, as likely as not take the final form of a thrashing for the police. LYNCHING FEVER IN LOUISIANA. A Mob About to Hang a Negro for an Offense He Didn't Commit.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 4.—A mob of 100 armed men dragged a negro from the Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific train at Rayville, La., and were about to hang him to a neighboring tree on the ground that he had slapped a white woman, Mrs. Alien Sholars, at Monroe.

Some person suggested to the mob that as Mr. Sholars himself was on the train he could give an account of the outrage. When he was found he explained that it was all a mistake, that in a scrimmage at the Monroe station his nurse had been knocked down, probably by the police, in trying to make an arrest, and that the negro who was about to be lynched was entirely innocent of any offense. He was allowed to leave on the train, paralyzed by fright at his narrow escape from lynching.
